item.title: China’s New Tunnel-Boring Export Controls Cast Shadow Over Warming Ties With India
item.description: Despite the warming ties between China and India following President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, trade frictions and territorial tensions continue to simmer beneath the surface. China announced sweeping new export controls on tunnel-boring machines and other specialized …
item.dc:creator: Rudy Lu
item.content:encoded:
Despite the warming ties between China and India following President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, trade frictions and territorial tensions continue to simmer beneath the surface.

China announced sweeping new export controls on tunnel-boring machines and other specialized construction equipment last week, a move Chinese analysts have interpreted as an attempt to restrict India’s strategic infrastructure development, particularly along the countries’ disputed Himalayan border.

The regulations, issued jointly by the Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs , cover tunnel-boring machines (TBMs), including shield machines and hard-rock tunnel borers, as well as critical components such as cutterheads, main drive systems and remanufacturing technologies. They also extend to specialized walking excavators capable of operating in difficult terrain and concrete-spraying machines used to reinforce tunnels at high altitudes.

The equipment is widely used in civilian infrastructure projects, such as metro systems, high-speed railways, highways, and hydropower facilities. The same machines can also be used to build military transport corridors, strategic tunnels, and other infrastructure supporting troop and equipment movements in mountainous border regions.

Set to take effect on November 18, the rules establish a two-tier export approval system.

Exporters shipping covered equipment to what Beijing describes as “sensitive countries and regions that have disputes with China” must obtain government licenses. Shipments to other destinations are subject to a simpler registration process.

Overseas organizations and individuals are prohibited from transferring or supplying Chinese-origin controlled equipment to sensitive destinations without Beijing’s approval, potentially affecting international contractors that purchase machinery in one country and redeploy it elsewhere.

Beijing has not publicly identified which countries fall under the sensitive-destination category.

The announcement has raised concerns in India, where major infrastructure projects remain dependent on imported tunneling equipment. According to a 2020 investigation by The Indian Express , industry suppliers estimated that nearly 90 percent of tunnel-boring machines deployed across India had links to China..

India’s Economic Times reported that government officials plan to consult industry stakeholders to mitigate the potential impact . While officials played down the likelihood of widespread delays to highway construction, they acknowledged that shortages of specialized machinery could affect major projects, such as the Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed railway, India’s first under-construction high-speed bullet train project.

New Delhi has already begun efforts to reduce its dependence on imported equipment.

Reuters reported in August that India was preparing a $1.2 billion manufacturing incentive program aimed at attracting $1.8 billion in investment over seven years. Tunnel-boring machines are among the priority products.

Li Guangman, a senior researcher at the Kunlunce Research Institute, a leftist, pro-government Chinese think tank, said that restricting tunnel-boring equipment would allow Beijing to constrain India’s construction of military transport networks near the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border separating Indian-controlled territory from Chinese-controlled territory.

Bloomberg reported in August that India is planning to invest $4.7 billion in railway upgrades along its borders with China, Pakistan and Bangladesh over the next two years. Li argued that advanced tunneling machinery could help India build all-weather transport corridors through the Himalayas, allowing troops and military supplies to move more easily across the mountainous frontier.

The restrictions also come amid renewed territorial friction. India’s Home Ministry announced early this month standardized names for 28 locations and geographical features in Ladakh, including areas disputed with China.

China’s Foreign Ministry firmly opposed the announcement , reiterating that Beijing has never recognized the “so-called Union Territory of Ladakh,” which India had established “unilaterally and illegally.”
